Zambia’s Economy Faces Setbacks Amid Severe Influenza Outbreak

LUSAKA—Zambia’s economic activity has slowed sharply as the country grapples with a severe influenza outbreak prompting nationwide health measures, including school closures and limits on public gatherings. The Ministry of Health reported over 180,000 confirmed cases of the H5N8 influenza strain since early May, with hospitals in Lusaka, Ndola, and Kitwe experiencing record admissions.

President Godfrey Banda’s administration announced restrictions last week, ordering the closure of schools, universities, cinemas, and sports venues for an initial three weeks. Markets and non-essential businesses are operating under reduced hours, while inter-provincial travel faces new curbs. “We recognize the economic impact, but our priority is saving lives,” Health Minister Dr. Ruth Chanda said in a televised address.

The measures have hit Zambia’s retail, transport, and hospitality sectors. The Zambia National Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimates that daily retail turnover has fallen by 35% since restrictions began. “Our members, especially small traders, are struggling to stay afloat,” said Chamber President James Mwamba.

Mining operations, a mainstay of Zambia’s export economy, continue but with reduced staffing. However, supply chain disruptions are slowing copper shipments. “There is a backlog at the border and at ports, which is affecting cash flow for exporters,” said Peter Mweene, an analyst at Lusaka-based Tashika Capital.

The kwacha fell 2.1% against the US dollar over the past week, with traders citing concerns over prolonged disruptions and lower tax revenues. The Bank of Zambia has urged calm, stating it stands ready to intervene if market volatility accelerates.

Labour unions are calling for urgent income support. “Workers in affected sectors need help now,” said Lillian Phiri, general secretary of the Union of Informal Workers. The government has yet to announce any stimulus or relief package.
